Exploring the troubling temporalities produced by fetal personhood

Katie Gentile

Katie Gentile

USA

Katie Gentile   About the AuthorKatie Gentile is Associate Professor of Counseling and Director of the Gender Studies Program at John Jay College of Criminal Justice. She is co-editor of the journal Studies in Gender and Sexuality and author of the forthcoming The Business of Being Born: Integrating Cultural and Psychoanalytic Theories to Explore the Production of Temporalities in Assisted Reproductive Technologies (Routledge).
fetish, time, fetal personhood, queer temporality, risk management

This paper integrates queer and psychoanalytic theories of temporality to explore the raft of new laws and resulting cases that imbue the fetus with status as a person. The laws increasingly result in women being depicted as in a liminal state of “could be pregnant,” thus, as objects of heightened medical and social surveillance. Exploring the affective dynamics of the culture, I show that fetuses embody displaced anxieties and vulnerabilities such that fetal protection functions to reinforce dissociation. It becomes clear that fetal personhood laws reflect a form of temporally-based affect regulation in which the fetus comes to embody the promise of an otherwise tenuous future. Regulation is enacted through a criminal-justice–based form of future-oriented risk management that takes poor women and women of color as its main targets.

Rosemary Rizq

Rosemary Rizq

UK

Rosemary Rizq  

audit culture, IAPT, NHS, organisational dynamics, perversion, psychoanalysis

Recent psychosocial and organisational literature has illuminated how perverse social defences and systemic failures within institutions can act to undermine the work of an organisation. In this paper, I draw on psychoanalytic theory to consider the notions of perversion and fetishisation within the context of contemporary UK public mental health services which have been subject to New Public Management (NPM) restructuring. Illuminated by a case example based on my clinical experience within an expanded NHS mental health service, I explore how services that are subject to neoliberal regulatory and performance management systems sponsor a perverse organisational solution to the anxieties and difficulties of dealing with psychologically distressed patients.

Arab Spring, granted self, phantasy, identity, narcissism, abjection

This paper analyses the evolution of Western perceptions of the Arab Spring through the prism of self/other identities and psychoanalysis. Reconstructing the process of perception, the argument suggests that the West engages in a self-pleasing phantasy of first recognising itself in protesters, and then, when faced with irreconcilable difference, developing a no less narcissistic suspicion. The argument is situated in the broader dynamics of self-definition against the unknown, and the illusions and traumas of a meaningful discovery of the other.

The mother in the age of mechanical reproduction: Psychoanalysis, photography, deconstruction

Amy Ray Stewart

Amy Ray Stewart

USA

Amy Ray Stewart  

Elissa Marder Fordham University Press, New York, 2012, 306pp., paper, $27.00, ISBN: 978-0-8232-4056-2; cloth, $80.00, ISBN: 978-0-8232-4055-5

The cryptic figure of the mother, one might say, marks the very birth of psychoanalysis. Elissa Marder’s The Mother in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction: Psychoanalysis, Photography, Deconstruction returns to the primal scene of birth in order to offer scholars a lucid account of the uncanny status of the maternal function – that which bears recurrent anxieties regarding the excluded memory of birth – within psychoanalysis, photography, and literature. Marder’s brilliant analysis of what she calls the “mechanical reproductions” of the maternal function within culture and society indicates the limitless milieu within which modern technologies usurp the maternal body in order to contain ostensibly uncontainable anxieties over maternal abjection and loss (p. 5). Insofar as culture is permeated with traces of the maternal function, Marder’s own conception of the mother in the age of mechanical reproduction demands a philosophical, if not psychoanalytic, theorization of the uncanny aporia of birth and the maternal body. Despite this intimacy and exile that characterize the subject’s relation to the event of birth, Marder suggests that the spectral presence of the mother, through language and imagination, facilitates the transformation of impossibilities into imaginable futures.

Marder carefully organizes her book into three distinct, yet interrelated, parts (each of which is constituted by four chapters) that respectively emphasize the spectral trace of the maternal function within psychoanalytic discourse, photographic technologies, and literature. Here, it is fascinating that, while Marder never directly attributes her categorical organization to Kristeva, each of these categories (psychoanalysis, photography, and literature) indirectly appears in a striking passage from Black Sun, in which Kristeva (1987) declares that “upon losing [the] mother… I retrieve her as sign, image, word” (p. 63). For Kristeva, the abjected maternal body may be recovered through the semiotic emerging within the symbolic inasmuch as the figure of the mother as the “repressed other can safely make its way back into our psyches and society through language” (Oliver, 1998, p. 97). In continuity with Kristeva’s thought, then, Marder’s book traces the maternal function as it emerges through “sign, image, word” via the signifiers within psychoanalysis, the photographic and filmic images of culture, and the very bits of language found in literature.

USA

Lynn Makau  

slavery, trauma, white guilt, postracial mythologies

Discussions of America’s history of slavery can lead to paralysis in contemporary audiences who prefer the wish-fulfilling fantasy of films like Django Unchained that, like myths of a postracial society, suppress the trauma of this history and its ongoing legacy. The slave narratives, historical fiction and secondary materials in my course, “Peculiar Intimacies,” counter such depictions and enable students to move past their stultifying guilt toward productive analysis of trauma and its repercussions. A recent class led a public forum on Tarantino’s Django to encourage discussion and awareness of our affective responses to historical trauma rather than their suppression.

[[RunningHead]]

Psychoanalysis and ecology at the edge of chaos: Complexity theory, Deleuze/Guattari and psychoanalysis for a climate in crisis

Robert Tollemache

Robert Tollemache

UK

Robert Tollemache  

Joseph Dodds, Routledge, London, 2011, 238pp., £80 (hardcover), £19.99 (paper), ISBN: 978-0415666121.

In 1972 Harold Searles challenged the psychoanalytic world, suggesting that the lack of environmental thinking within psychoanalysis might be caused by destructive unconscious factors. Since his call for a psychoanalytic environmental debate, the psychoanalytic movement has remained largely silent, until Joseph Dodds’s recent response. In this review I will describe how Dodds understands the relationship between psychoanalysis and climate change, as well as how he sees complexity theory and self-organisation as adding to psychoanalytic understanding.

Dodds maintains that ‘the new nomadic sciences of complexity, combined with the philosophy of Deleuze and Guattari, help to provide a framework … for thinking our way out of extinction’ (p. 183). He believes that the crisis of potential future climate catastrophe calls for the introduction of non-linear, ecological thinking to psychoanalysis, and of psychoanalysis into ecology; the environment is present but silent in psychoanalysis. Michael Balint, in The Basic Fault described ‘a harmonious interpenetrating mix-up’ (1989, pp. 67–68), where the object is taken for granted, just as we assume the ongoing supply of air. Psychoanalysis is essentially concerned with the internal world, including internal object relationships, and lacks a common conceptual framework for exploring the relationship of the individual and the group with the natural world, so it has disregarded environmental issues.

Dodds suggests ways of understanding psychoanalytic ideas and their relationship to nature and the environment. Freud saw civilisation as opposed to nature. Dodds draws on the philosophers Gilles Deleuze and Felix Guattari (who was also a psychoanalyst) to show us the interconnectedness between the ecology of mind, the ecology of society and the ecology of nature; each is a world of infinite complexity. Following Deleuze and Guattari, who see mind, society and nature as a continuum, separated only for clarity, Dodds locates psychoanalysis as part of a mind-society-nature continuum. This interconnectedness with nature goes against our psychoanalytic practice, where we try to exclude the outside world, and to provide a secure frame, through dependability, calm, confidentiality, and continuity, within the consulting room. In a changing world, we provide the illusion of stability.

Feminine look: Sexuation, spectatorship, subversion

Esther Rashkin

Esther Rashkin

USA

Esther Rashkin  

Jennifer Friedlander, SUNY Press, Albany, New York, 2008, 139 pp., $24.95, ISBN-13: 978-0791472965

In recent years, the major emphasis of psychoanalytically oriented scholarship engaged with Lacan’s concept of the Real (understood as what lies beyond the signifier and the symbolic order) has been on trauma and the way it eludes representation and infects the subject with a sense of haunting anxiety. In her refreshing and thought-provoking book, Feminine Look: Sexuation, Spectatorship, Subversion, Jennifer Friedlander shifts the focus from the relationship between trauma and the Real to that between visuality and the Real. Her purpose is to articulate a new feminist psychoanalytic theory of spectatorship that challenges previous ways of considering the connections between looking and pleasure, and between spectatorship and ideology. By linking Lacan’s concept of sexuation, presented in his Seminar XX Encore: On Feminine Sexuality: The Limits of Love and Knowledge (1972-1973), as the way in which the signifier positions the subject between the sexes, with Roland Barthes’s concept of the punctum, elaborated in his highly influential essay on photography, Camera Lucida (1980), Friedlander proposes a fascinating alternative to extant theories of feminist spectatorship that hinge on sexual difference and the refusal of moments of “pleasure and surprise” (p. 5). Her concern, by contrast, is to show how certain spectatorial events actually depend on such pleasurable and unexpected moments.

Key to Friedlander’s project is her view that Barthes’s Camera Lucida has been mistakenly interpreted as a rejection of poststructuralist thinking and as a nostalgic return to realism. In her intriguing rereading of the work, she understands Barthes’s description of the punctum – the apparently banal, accidental detail that disrupts the studium or culturally expected interpretation of a photograph – as an uncoded, uncanny “point of non-meaning” (p. 13) that moves the image beyond nature as well as culture and “thus operates at the level of Lacan’s Real” (p. 13). She explores this Barthesian/Lacanian nexus through her close readings of three photographs by André Kertész. Each of these images illustrates the complex relationship between realism and the photographic accident. As Friedlander demonstrates, however, the accidents captured in each photograph are very different with respect to their formal, aesthetic, sociopolitical, and autobiographical functions.

Amy Stewart

Amy Stewart   About the AuthorAmy Ray Stewart is a PhD student in the Department of Philosophy at Southern Illinois University Carbondale, where she teaches Women, Gender, and Sexuality Studies. Her research specializations include Kristevan and Lacanian psychoanalytic thought, feminist continental philosophy, and gender/cultural studies. Lacan, Kristeva, psychoanalysis, lynching photography, racial violence

This article engages Lacanian and Kristevan psychoanalysis to examine lynching photographs and picture postcards that were disseminated throughout the southern United States between 1890 and 1940. I argue that these photographs are not only archival objects intended to incite racial terrorization and propagate white supremacy, but also unstable signifiers that expose the concerted méconnaissance of whiteness as wholeness. Introducing the concept of the abject stain, I indicate how lynching photographs inaugurate an unsettling encounter with the extimate horror of racial alterity, which is experienced as an intimate ethics of witnessing.

The effects of neoliberal practices have spread like a wave through Brazil. In Brazilian schools, they have materialized in a variety of forms. I will specifically address the policy that restricts options for keeping back students with learning difficulties. Sasha Roseneil   About the AuthorSasha Roseneil is Professor of Sociology and Social Theory and Director of the Birkbeck Institute for Social Research at Birkbeck, University of London and Professor II at the Centre for Gender Research at the University of Oslo. She has written widely on social politics, social movements and citizenship, and gender, sexuality and intimacy, and the relationship of all of these with processes of social, cultural and political transformation. Her recent books include Social Research beyond the Cultural Turn (co-edited with Stephen Frosh, Palgrave, 2012), Remaking Citizenship in Multicultural Europe: Women’s Movements, Gender and Diversity (co-edited with Beatrice Halsaa and Sevil Sumer, Palgrave, 2012) and Beyond Citizenship? Feminism and the Transformation of Belonging (Palgrave, 2013).
belonging, welfare state, intimacy, ethical relationality, animals, individualisation

This paper begins with an ‘experience-near’ account of the author’s encounter with a woman she met whilst walking her dog in an east London park one winter afternoon. The woman was lying on the ground amongst the trees and, when approached, talked with the author about her feelings of isolation from family and community, about her alcoholism, suicidality and unsuccessful attempts to access help from the welfare state, and about the connections to animals and nature that kept her alive. The paper goes on to offer a psychoanalytically informed psychosocial commentary on this meeting and on the human relational vulnerability of which it speaks, exploring what we might learn about belonging and not belonging in the contemporary conjuncture, as welfare spending is cut, economic inequalities increase, and the ‘social investment state’ targets the ‘worthy’ welfare subject at the expense of people like Linda. The paper discusses the resonances between Linda’s life as glimpsed through this encounter and the author’s recent psychosocial research on intimacy and care under conditions of individualisation and detraditionalisation. Through this, the paper explores the practices of ethical relationality that are at the heart of the individual’s struggle to belong and through which social belonging is created.

Bob Samuels

Bob Samuels   About the AuthorBob Samuels is President of the University Council-American Federation of Teachers. He teaches Writing and Media Studies at UCSB, and he is the author of seven books, including the forthcoming Why Public Higher Education Should be Free (Rutgers Press, 2013).
neoliberalism, narcissism, obsessional, meritocracy, ideological critique, higher education

While some blame most of the problems of higher education on the neoliberal cutting of taxes, reduced public spending, and corporatization, this paper argues that ideological criticism leaves out the role played by individuals in creating and maintaining a system of gross inequality. In order to comprehend neoliberalism, it is necessary to understand how all of the classic liberal institutions – unions, universities, and the Democratic Party – have been undermined from within. Many liberals are able to escape recognizing their role in neoliberalism by blaming larger social forces; instead, from a psychoanalytic perspective, this paper examines why and how people promote systems that lead to their own oppression. To explain this type of liberal complicity, the theory of obsessional narcissism is developed. Central to this theory is the idea that the more people suffer from lost opportunities and social inequality, the more they seek to become winners in the system that oppresses them. Part of this theory comes from the idea that underlying the narcissistic need for approval from others is a repressed unconscious sense of nothingness or low self-esteem.

Roger Frie

Roger Frie

Canada

Roger Frie   About the AuthorRoger Frie is Professor of Education at Simon Fraser University, Affiliate Professor of Psychiatry, University of British Columbia (both in Vancouver, Canada) and Faculty and Supervisor at the William Alanson White Institute of Psychiatry, Psychoanalysis, and Psychology in New York and the Institute of Contemporary Psychoanalysis in Los Angeles. He has published six books on the intersection of psychoanalysis, philosophy and social theory and is completing a book on German memory and the Holocaust. He is Co-Editor of the International Journal of Psychoanalytic Self Psychology, Associate Editor of Contemporary Psychoanalysis and Editorial Board Member of Psychoanalytic Psychology.
German memory, Holocaust, narrative, hermeneutics, shame, silence

This article considers the relationship between traumatic history, narrative memory and the limits of understanding. It suggests that inherited traumatic memory is transmitted in family narratives that remain unconsciously organized and are guided by affective and dissociative processes. The author draws on autobiographical experience, particularly his German family’s own narrative of the Nazi past and the Holocaust. He suggests that what we remember or forget, what we know or do not know, is inherently connected to the narratives we inherit and rely on to make sense of the world. Using a hermeneutic perspective, he demonstrates the role of silence and of emotional processes, such as shame, which lead to the unconscious reproduction of family narratives. Until narratives and their affective processes are consciously organized, their meanings remain inherently ambiguous. The article shows how this ambiguity is powerfully at work in the German response to the perpetration and the traumas of the Holocaust. The author concludes by suggesting that a meaningful moral response to the Nazi past must account for both an articulated history and the feelings bound up in inherited memories, thus opening up a space for dialogue, acceptance and the creation of new narratives.

Jason Glynos   About the AuthorJason Glynos teaches political theory at the Department of Government, University of Essex. He has published in the areas of poststructuralist political theory and Lacanian psychoanalysis, focusing on theories of ideology, democracy, and freedom, and the philosophy and methodology of social science. He is co-author of Logics of Critical Explanation in Social and Political Theory (Routledge, 2007), and co-editor of Politics and the Unconscious (Special Issue of Subjectivity, 2010).
neoliberalism, markets, fantasy, health, over-investment, contingency

In this paper I explore one psychoanalytically inspired reason why we might worry about policies that aim to maximise market competition and user choice in some areas of social life. Using the case of health and social care, I suggest that the spread of neoliberalised practices would amplify splitting tendencies in subjects that subscribe to particular fantasies, for example, independence fantasies of ‘Individual Self-Sufficiency’ or dependence fantasies of the ‘Caring Other’. One of psychoanalysis’s strongest critical contributions resides in its effort to show what such fantasies have in common: the potential to secure allegiance through the promise of a subjective suture that results in fantasmatic over-investment. Such a perspective points to the rather urgent need to identify and promote those wider cultural and structural conditions that militate against fantasmatic over-investment and toward forms of interdependence that acknowledge contingency and ambivalence.

Lacan, language, jouissance, mysticism, Zen Buddhism, individualisation

Language is at the core of Lacanian theory. It is the advent of language and the ‘law of the father’ which leads from the presymbolic full jouissance to the subject’s partial jouissance – a state which always entails division, permanent lack and alienation. I argue that Lacanians should take more seriously into account a type of religious or secular spirituality which aims, via meditative techniques, at bracketing or suspending language and thinking for short or long periods of time. When this is achieved alienation and permanent lack seem to subside. In such cases should we speak of a postsymbolic spiritual jouissance? Questions about meditation and the symbolic are crucial given that, due to widespread individualisation, meditative practices are expanding rapidly in late modernity.

I’m not black, I’m not white, what am I? The illusion of the color line

Daniel Gaztambide

Daniel Gaztambide

USA

Daniel Gaztambide  

race, black checking, color line, the Real, object map

Discussions of the racial “color line” in the United States are often framed in terms of “Black and White,” addressing the historical subjugation and oppression of African-Americans, the dynamics of White privilege, and the relationship between the two. Although a necessary point of critical inquiry, what is at times lost in these conversations are the ways in which the color line functions as an illusion which reifies – and in fact codifies – an unconscious construction in which racial discussions have only two terms, Black and White. Black or Blackness, and White or Whiteness, refer to specific cultural, social, and identity performances which exclude other racialized experiences (for example, Latinos, Asians, South Asians, etc.) as well as those subjectivities which do not fit neatly into their presumed racial identifications (for example, African Americans who are “not Black enough”). Taking my own experience of Latino ethnic ambiguity as a source of data, I will argue that two perpendicular conversations need to be entertained. On the one hand a critical analysis of race and the influence of anti-Black racism and colorism is a necessary, but insufficient, source of emancipatory politics. What is needed in addition to this discourse is a discussion of ways of performing racial/ethnic identification that does not conform to established constructs of “Black and White.” I theorize that a renewal of emancipatory energy can take place at the intersection of these two discourses.

Dušan Bjelić

Dušan Bjelić

USA

Dušan Bjelić  

Julia Kristeva, Translated by Jeanine Herman Columbia University Press, New York, 2010, 341 pp., $29.50. ISBN-10: 0231143257

Hatred and Forgiveness is a compilation of Kristeva’s public lectures, conference papers and interviews concerned with a variety of issues such as daily politics, psychoanalysis, religion, women, writing, fatigue, anorexia and the arts. All these issues stem from the same premise: at a time of globalization, nationalism and Islamic fundamentalism, psychoanalysis is the only path to psychic salvation.

Even though the book comprises an assortment of fragments from Kristeva’s professional appearances, the sequential order of the six thematic chapters (World(s), Women, Psychoanalysis, Religion, Portraits, and Writing) structures the fragments as a continuous analysis, which starts with diagnoses of global psychic illness, moves to the intimate, and ends with the arts and writing as the path to what Kristeva describes as “psychical rebirth” (p. 158).

The opening chapter, “Thinking About Liberty in Dark Times,” sets up the diagnostic context for the rest of the book: we are living in “Dark Times,” trapped between Islamic fundamentalism and American financial oligarchy; America is becoming a new Rome, which as a consequence creates global reaction in the form of ethnic nationalism and political radicalism. Europe offers “an alternative to the globalized world” (p. 17) that emphasizes the particular “art of living, taste, leisure, the so-called ‘idle’ pleasures, grace, pure chance, playfulness, wastefulness, our ‘dark side’ even, or, to put it in a nutshell, freedom as the essence of ‘Being-in-the-World’ prior to any ‘Cause’” (p. 17).

Premising the modern subject as a work-in-progress of self-opening, she focuses on woman and singles out throughout the book what she considers the three major causes of woman’s foreclosure, or the “veiling of women”: totalitarianism; Islam; and bisexuality. According to Kristeva, because France lacks proper social policies to promote gender equality and protect physically and mentally disabled individuals (like Kristeva’s own son), French universalism fails to deliver on its promises of equality for all. The inclusion of the most vulnerable subjects into French society would open it to the productive force of the “Feminine Genius” (p. 17) and to the psychic politics of maternal charity. Gender inequality and women’s disenfranchisement are merely the external manifestations of women’s psychic and cultural foreclosure, a foreclosure that is, for Kristeva, also evident in Islam.

Jason Glynos   About the AuthorJason Glynos teaches Political Theory at the Department of Government, University of Essex. He has published in the areas of poststructuralist political theory and Lacanian psychoanalysis, focusing on theories of ideology, democracy, and freedom, and the philosophy and methodology of social science. He is co-author of Logics of Critical Explanation in Social and Political Theory (Routledge, 2007), and co-editor of Politics and the Unconscious (Special Issue of Subjectivity, 2010).
self-transgression, enjoyment, fantasy, ideology, orthogonality, critique

The psychoanalytic contribution to our understanding of hating government and voting against our own interests can be appreciated by invoking the categories of fantasy and enjoyment. Essential to the psychoanalytic enterprise is the idea that there is no necessary relation between a subject’s investment in a fantasmatic narrative and how faithfully this narrative reflects a consensus reality. As a prominent narrative element in political discourse, ‘big government’ can thus play for the subject two analytically distinct roles: an ideological role (linked to our fantasmatic investment in the world) and an epistemological role (linked to our understanding of the world). I argue that an appeal to fantasy not only helps us better grasp this difference in roles, but also enables us to appreciate its social and political implications.

Ronnie Lesser   About the AuthorRonnie C. Lesser is a psychoanalyst who maintains practices in Lyme, New Hampshire and Norwich, Vermont. She is co-editor with Thomas Domenici of Disorienting Sexuality: Psychoanalytic Reappraisals of Sexual Identities (Routledge, 1995) and co-editor with Erica Schoenberg of That Obscure Object of Desire: Freud’s Female Homosexual Revisited (Routledge, 1999).
psychoanalysis, neoliberalisms, critique, developmentalism, mutual respect

This paper attempts to demonstrate the inextricability of the sociopolitical from the clinical practice of working with patients, by presenting a brief vignette of a session that took place immediately after I listened to a news broadcast. Because I view psychoanalytic theory and practice as inseparable from sociopolitical reality, I propose that psychoanalysis is an approach to living that is grounded in culture and values. I argue that by espousing a view of psychoanalysis as truth, we inadvertently contribute to naturalizing neoliberalism. I also attempt to broaden our view of neoliberal subjectivities.

After a brief description of the ethical turn and its historical-political dimension within psychoanalysis, this article will introduce the special issue’s four papers and two responses, all of which were presented at the 2013 Psychology and the Other Conference. These articles represent substantive additions to the burgeoning literature highlighting the intersections of ethical phenomenology, hermeneutics, psychoanalysis and political life. Matthew Adams   About the AuthorMatthew Adams is a Principal Lecturer in the School of Applied Social Sciences at the University of Brighton. He is currently working with colleagues at Brighton in developing a psychosocial approach to the sustainability and pro-environmental behaviour agenda, and on a monograph for Palgrave provisionally titled Voice, Narrative and Resistance: Subjectivity and the Limits of Language. He has published widely on the themes of social change, subjectivity, reflexivity, class, consumption and culture.
consumerism, Dark Mountain Project, defence mechanisms, denial, social organisation of denial, sustainability

The evidence that we face a catalogue of environmental crises caused by human activities, which pose a threat to planetary, social and personal continuity, is communicated in increasingly sophisticated ways. Despite increased knowledge, the populaces of wealthy nations appear to be outwardly ignoring such risks, continuing their consumption patterns unabated, and failing to mount a significant public response. Interventions aimed at encouraging more sustainable behaviours have largely drawn on individualistic psychology, and to date they have been largely unsuccessful. This paper is a call to deepen and widen our understanding of the psychosocial processes involved in not responding to the issues at stake. It does so by drawing on narrative approaches in the social sciences, psychoanalytic conceptualisations of defence mechanisms, and recent work addressing the social organisation of denial. The potential of these developments for informing social movements and political action is briefly considered in the light of an example, the Dark Mountain Project.

Mari Ruti

Mari Ruti

Mari Ruti   About the AuthorMari Ruti is Professor of Critical Theory at the University of Toronto, where she teaches contemporary theory, continental philosophy, and psychoanalysis. She is the author of several books, most recently The Singularity of Being: Lacan and the Immortal Within (2012) and The Call of Character: Living a Life Worth Living (2013).
Lacan, Marcuse, desire, surplus-repression, the ethical act, revolutionary politics

This essay brings Lacan into conversation with Marcuse to investigate the link between “deviant” desires and the inclination for personal and collective acts of resistance. Offering a Lacanian-Marcusian counterpoint to the Foucauldian-Butlerian notion that resistance is a matter of negotiating with disciplinary power, the essay explains the political stakes of the so-called Lacanian “act” – of following the “truth” of one’s desire even at the risk of one’s symbolic intelligibility. In a culture that fetishizes intersubjectivity, such an act of severing social bonds may seem like the very antithesis of ethics, yet – from a specifically Lacanian perspective – it is the culmination of ethics as well as (potentially at least) an opening to radical social change.

This paper is a brief, psychoanalytically informed exploration of youth development, with a focus on the often-negative psychosocial impact of neoliberal ideologies on low-income Black youth. Neoliberal policies have influenced the psychological development of low-income Black youths, who are embedded in psychosocial contexts that are often under-resourced and negatively racialized. This substantially constrains their attempts to love and work. There is often a paucity of safe places, identity capital and caring tutors of the imagination that might facilitate good outcomes for these young people. As a consequence of being embedded in such emotionally austere and unsafe places, they often adopt postures that lead to their under-development and, too often, their early demise. The paper also discusses some strategies of resistance to neoliberal ideology and policy.

In the last three decades, neoliberalism has come to dominate most of the West, reshaping many institutions according to its ideological belief in markets as the optimal form of regulation of social and economic life. Whereas formerly market ideology was contested by collectivist ideas of the public good, at this point of its triumph there is little systemic opposition to it. Does psychoanalysis have distinctive insights to offer on neoliberalism, and if so, can they contribute to contesting its domination? Two starting points for such a critique are the relational ideas that are the foundations of psychoanalytic object-relations approaches, and the post-Kleinian theory of narcissism. object fear, race/racism, relational psychoanalysis, President Obama, ethical third, racial unconscious

This paper furthers the use of psychoanalysis as a lens for reading the contemporary political and social world and explores the ongoing reproduction of the racial unconscious in the United States. In applying a psychoanalytic lens to interpersonal violence and legal and political discourse during Obama’s presidency, we attempt to explore how internal fear of blackness prevents America and psychoanalysis from accessing non-destructive relational psychological spaces. We argue that the violent responses to racial blackness and power are not second-hand effects of racial and economic disparity, but rather intimate parts of our psychodynamics that involve an intersubjective process we term “object fear.” We discuss relational theories that help us negotiate object fear as a location for often ignored racialized group and dyadic psychodynamics, looking at specific examples of object fear, interpersonal violence and the limits of relational psychoanalysis to address these types of object relations. We end by turning to a series of recent Supreme Court decisions to look at the ways in which object fear has been triggered at this historical moment in relation to the presence of a black president and the threat to the maintenance of white supremacy in the United States.

During African-American slavery, the rape of slave women by their masters was ubiquitous. This unrecognized atrocity shaped the US economy and has informed race relations. This history is written into the skin of US analysts, but it has not penetrated psychoanalytic theory, practice, or consciousness. My article traces the historical abuse of slave women’s bodies and the transgenerational effects of the exploitation. This tracing proceeds through an intimate look at the author’s personal analysis, in which she, a Russian-Jewish patient, is treated by a light-skinned African-American analyst. In the transference, the history of slavery emerges: the analyst’s apparent whiteness echoes with rape on the plantation. Racial guilt and conflict is worked through motifs of loss, forced separation, and internalized racism.

Freud, Medusa, c-word, Hoffman, female genitalia, feminism

This paper revisits Freud's famous posthumous essay on "Medusa's Head" in light of a recent "cunt-roversy" at the University of Colorado, Boulder, where a scandal erupted involving the remark made in deposition by the female President of the University (during an allegation against the university) that defended the "c-word" as neither "vile" nor "disgusting." Mark Freeman

Mark Freeman

USA

Mark Freeman   About the AuthorMark Freeman is Chair and Professor of Psychology and Distinguished Professor of Ethics and Society at the College of the Holy Cross in Worcester, Massachusetts. His writings include Rewriting the Self: History, Memory, Narrative; Hindsight: The Promise and Peril of Looking Backward; The Priority of the Other: Thinking and Living Beyond the Self, and numerous articles on issues ranging from memory and identity to the psychology of art and religion. Winner of the 2010 Theodore R. Sarbin Award from the Society for Theoretical and Philosophical Psychology, he is also a Fellow of the American Psychological Association and serves as editor for the Oxford University Press series “Explorations in Narrative Psychology.”
holocaust, moral life, narrative, shame, trauma, unconscious

This article offers commentary on Roger Frie’s “Limits of understanding: Psychological experience, German memory, and the Holocaust.” Specifically, the article presents four variants of unconsciousness pertinent to Frie’s work: the dynamic unconscious, as articulated in classical psychoanalysis; the narrative unconscious, which is about those culturally-rooted aspects of our histories that have yet to become an explicit part of our life stories; the temporal unconscious, manifested especially in the form of our “lateness” in understanding and coming to terms with the past; and the ethical unconscious, which, for present purposes, refers to the call made upon us by others and often manifested in the form of guilt or shame over our own inaction or inability adequately to respond to it. That in the case of the Holocaust it is literally too late to respond to such a call is largely irrelevant. The call remains, and painful though it may be to hear it now, it stands as an important index of our frequently unacknowledged humanity.

[[RunningHead]]

The fantasy of feminist history

Patricia Ingham

Patricia Ingham

USA

Patricia Ingham  

Joan Wallach Scott, Duke University Press, Durham and London, 2011, vii plus 187 pp., $22.95, ISBN-13: 978-0822351252

“I’d rather be dead than misread,” confesses Joan Wallach Scott in the epilogue to the important essays gathered together in The Fantasy of Feminist History. Of course, as the essays themselves testify and as Scott well knows, the two rhyming signifiers of this culminating avowal are not exactly alternatives to one another. And if none of us can escape the first fate, feminist theorists and historians may be particularly bound to suffer the second. The epilogue – her final meditation on “A Feminist Theory Archive” – pertains at least in part to the archive of Scott’s own work, attesting to the personal and political stakes in the problem posed by the title of her collection. Fantasy serves as a powerful analytic category for feminist history; psychoanalytic methods of reading illuminate history and culture, helping to unhook the categories of sexual difference from certain recursive prevailing assumptions. But these fantasies also impinge on feminism’s own, and Scott also troubles any strictly evolutionary account of the enlightenment project of feminism as linked to full liberation or progress. Oriented around the category of fantasy, this collection of essays, thus, has a doubled force: it attends, on the one hand, to the transformative legacy of feminist academic labor in the waning decades of the twentieth century; on the other, The Fantasy of Feminist History confronts throughout the persistence of a darker aspect to fantasies of sexual difference circulating through and around feminism, including the reappearance of troubling versions of gender asymmetry that Scott has spent her entire career working to dismantle.

Scott’s groundbreaking blend of psychoanalytic theory and feminist historiography guided generations of scholars (myself included) in the ways and means of thinking historicism differently. She taught us to consider the interpenetration of important categories like difference with equality, and she lucidly deployed psychoanalytic protocols of reading to help us track such complications. A preeminent analyst of modern histories of gender and sexuality, Scott knows well the particular hermeneutic problems that attend archives (feminist, psychoanalytic, or historical) as well as the power of reading strategies capable of traversing recurrent fantasies of gender and sexuality, long analyzed and debated in psychoanalytic circles. And yet, as Scott’s long acquaintance with psychoanalytic theory has also taught her, fantasies of gender and sexuality are stubbornly persistent; indeed, psychoanalytic theory proves useful to her precisely as the “theory that posits sexual difference as an unresolvable dilemma” (p. 5). Those irresolutions might be understood to form the core of Scott’s meditations throughout this volume, and misreading is, in this context, something of a mixed blessing.

The fictional Christopher Nolan

Anna Kornbluh

Anna Kornbluh

USA

Anna Kornbluh  

Todd McGowan University of Texas Press, Austin, 2012, 232 pp., $55, ISBN-13: 978-0292737822

Unassumingly brilliant and surgically incisive, Todd McGowan’s recent monograph on the movies of Christopher Nolan, the unlikely director of both cult indie films like Memento and superhero-franchise international blockbusters like The Dark Knight, illustrates that Nolan’s impressively broad oeuvre actually comprises a consistent project to think cinematically about the mediation of truth by non-truths. Lies, deceit, illusions, and errors, far from being obstacles to or opposites of truth, are, for Nolan, preconditions of truth: “truth is the failure of the fiction” (p. 15). Linking this reversal to Hegelian philosophy and Freudian/Lacanian psychoanalysis, McGowan argues that Nolan’s insights are not only epistemologically consequential – bearing on how we can come to know ourselves and others, reality and the real – but also ethically charged. The ethics inhere in the practice of freedom that a lie discloses: “when we lie, we assert our freedom by detaching ourselves from the world as it is given to us” (p. 13). Such detachment activates a new relation to the world and possibilities for changing it: when the world is not sanctified, no transcendent beyond of the world is necessary for reform or revolution; hewing to fictionality exposes the fictionality of the world and invites new invention. “Believing in a real world of significance beyond the fantasy, we fail to act to change the structures in which we exist” (p. 17), but a cinema that aids the traversal of this belief can galvanize an ethics of fidelity to fundamental fantasies and a politics of new structures. Nolan’s cinema is not so much an example as the paradigm of this ethics, not so much a cinema as a meta-cinema – albeit one that avows the impossibility of meta-language. For while “the fundamental deception of cinema itself – the image passing itself off as reality” (p. 15) may function to perpetuate an image/reality opposition, Nolan’s works radicalize this deception: “the real deception is not that what we see on the screen is a reality but that there exists a real world beyond the screen” (p. 17). Unraveling this particular deception means fathoming the indispensability of the screen and embracing the truth of the lie, such that ultimately “recognizing the necessity of the foundational lie transforms the ground of our social interactions” (p. 82).

What is psychoanalysis? 100 years after Freud’s “secret committee”

Frank Summers

Frank Summers

USA

Frank Summers  

Barnaby Barratt, Routledge, London, 2012, 221 pp., ISBN: 978-0-69273-1; 978-0-415-69274-8; 978-0-203-09505-8

Barnaby Barrett believes that psychoanalysis was derailed in 1915 when Freud, upon Jones’s suggestion, formed a “secret committee” to protect the psychoanalytic turf. From that point forward, according to Barratt, analysis became focused on “keeping the faith” by committing its adherents to an ideology, preventing splinter groups, and consigning heretics to the category of apostasy. It was then that psychoanalysis lost its revolutionary spirit of inquiry and became a dogma, transforming Freud’s interests from the “interrogation of consciousness” to vague metapsychological explanation, resulting in the sectarianism of today’s analytic world.

The essence of the psychoanalytic revolution, for Barratt, was Freud’s discovery of the repressed unconscious and the way to “interrogate” it by free association. He endorses Freud’s statement that analysis is defined by its method of inquiry, not by content. When the process is permitted to flower, the four “coordinates” of analytic thought emerge: the repressed unconscious; the importance of personal history; Oedipal complexities; and bodily sensuality. Every post-1914 emendation to analytic thought, in Barratt’s view, is guilty of losing connection with the free associational method and at least three of the four “coordinates,” thereby watering down the power of Freud’s original ideas.

Most of the book is devoted to asserting the importance of the four coordinates and their role in the revolutionary process of psychoanalysis and to assailing all extant analytic schools for missing the essence of Freud’s revolution. According to Barratt, the maintenance of that spirit means openness to the polysemous nature of meaning as well as to polysexuality and pluritemporality. For example, he argues that psychoanalysis reveals that sexuality is inherently polymorphous, and it is only bourgeois ideology that constricts it to an endpoint in heterosexual intercourse. He sees Freud as torn between his sexual radicalism and adherence to cultural norms that Barratt regards as repressive.

Internal racism: A psychoanalytic approach to race and difference

Michelle Stephens and William Alanson

William Alanson

USA

USA

William Alanson  

M. Fakhry Davids Palgrave Macmillan, London, 2011, 254pp., $33.00, ISBN: 978-0333964576 (paperback)

A number of recent works at the intersection of cultural studies and psychoanalysis question the premium we have placed on human difference. In Flesh of My Flesh, Kaja Silverman (2009) points out that, “the notion that we cannot be ourselves unless we are different from everyone else is relatively new” (p. 1). Silverman, whose consistent engagement with psychoanalysis has defined her scholarship, reads Freud against the grain to uncover a discourse of sameness and affinity at the base of our understanding of subjective formation and relation. Vanita Seth (2010) confirms that our awareness of racial difference from the sixteenth century on diverged greatly from earlier European discourses structured around ideas of human resemblance. M. Fakhry Davids joins this discussion with a more clinically focused account, one that theorizes how difference gets both set up and deployed as a psychic structure in the normal mind.

Internal Racism presents a quite sophisticated account of how racism is inscribed in the mind as a paranoid defensive structure to ward off extreme anxiety. There are a number of radical premises in Davids’s misleadingly straightforward thesis, the first being that racism is a structure of the “normal” mind. As he asserts: “our model of the mind must be extended to incorporate a paranoid, us-them, construction involving self and racial other as a permanent feature” (p. 37). The racial other is the product of an object relationship that belongs to the same category of universal internal objects as “self, mother, father and superego” (p. 43). Davids’s second radical premise: our “sophisticated awareness of the social meanings of difference in the outside world” is not only historically produced, but has a developmental trajectory that can be mapped, for example, onto Freudian and Kleinian metapsychologies (p. 51). Weaving insights from object relations theory and Lacanian psychoanalysis, Davids describes the process by which a child’s splitting of parental caretakers into good and bad objects in infancy shifts to stranger anxiety and then to an awareness of an “out-group as the bad object” upon the waning of the Oedipus complex (p. 59). Reaching beyond psychoanalytic theory, he puts to excellent use Clark and Clark’s famous dolls study of the 1940 s, also drawing on more contemporary developmental research to substantiate this point.
